title: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (GRATK Treaty)

title: The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API)
section: Second Schedule, Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940; Rule 163-AA, Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945
summary: The official book of standards for the identity, purity and strength of Ayurvedic drugs, published in monographs by the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia Committee under the Pharmacopoeia Commission for Indian Medicine & Homoeopathy (PCIM&H), a subordinate office of the Ministry of AYUSH. Compliance with API standards is mandatory under the Second Schedule of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (as amended by Rule 163-AA, notified 22 March 2021) for any Ayurvedic drug manufactured or sold in India. Part I covers single-drug monographs (raw materials, herbal/mineral substances); Part II covers compound classical formulations also listed in the Ayurveda-relevant First Schedule authoritative texts. This is the concrete quality-standards layer beneath the classification question of whether a product is a 'classical/generic medicine' (§ per classifier.py) — a formulation matching an API monograph has a documented quality baseline a novel or proprietary formulation does not.

title: Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India & Ors.
section: Writ Petition (M/S) No. 3437 of 2017, High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital
summary: Decided 21 December 2018 (Sudhanshu Dhulia, J.). Baba Ramdev's Divya Pharmacy, an Indian-owned Ayurvedic manufacturer sourcing biological resources (herbs/plants) from Uttarakhand, challenged the Uttarakhand State Biodiversity Board's demand for a Fair and Equitable Benefit Sharing (FEBS) fee under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, arguing the Act's benefit-sharing duty applies only to entities with foreign participation. The Court dismissed the petition, holding that Sections 7 and 23 (read with Section 21) empower a State Biodiversity Board to demand benefit-sharing from any entity — Indian or foreign — commercially using biological resources sourced in India, and upheld the validity of the 2014 ABS Guidelines. Directly on point for the corpus's own ABS-compliance guidance (pathway.py's 'check NBA/State Biodiversity Board approval' step): it is the leading authority that an Ayurvedic manufacturer's Indian ownership does NOT exempt it from ABS/benefit-sharing obligations, a common misconception the classifier/pathway flow should not reinforce.
source_url: https://spicyip.com/2019/03/developing-bio-cultural-jurisprudence-for-securing-rights-of-indigenous-peoples-and-local-communities-divya-pharmacy-v-uoi.html (SpicyIP — detailed case analysis with direct quotations from the judgment)
authority: High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital

title: Directive 2004/24/EC — Traditional Herbal Medicinal Products (inserting Chapter 2a, Arts 16a–16i, into Directive 2001/83/EC)
section: Articles 16a–16i of Directive 2001/83/EC (as inserted by Directive 2004/24/EC)
summary: Creates the EU's simplified 'traditional-use registration' route for herbal medicinal products, so that an herbal product can be registered on long-standing use instead of a full clinical-trial dossier. Article 16a sets the criteria: indications appropriate to traditional products used without a doctor's supervision, a specified strength and posology, oral / external / inhalation use only, a sufficient period of traditional use, and plausible efficacy with no evidence of harm. Article 16b requires the applicant to be established in the Community. Article 16c requires evidence of at least 30 years of medicinal use, including at least 15 years within the Community (where EU use is shorter than 15 years but the product is otherwise eligible, the Member State refers the question to the Committee for Herbal Medicinal Products), plus quality data and a bibliographic safety review. Article 16h establishes the Committee for Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) at the European Medicines Agency, which prepares Community herbal monographs and the list of herbal substances. This is the registration regime relevant to exporting an Ayurvedic herbal product to the EU as a medicine; it is separate from, and does not replace, any IP filing or the EU's Nagoya due-diligence duties. Because at least 15 of the 30 years must be within the Community, a product whose traditional use is documented mainly outside the EU (as for many Ayurvedic products) may not qualify for this route without referral, and may need a different route such as a full or well-established-use marketing authorisation.
version_date: Directive 2004/24/EC of 31 March 2004 (OJ L 136, 30.4.2004, pp. 85–90); in force; implementation date 30 October 2005
authority: European Parliament and Council of the EU; administered by national competent authorities and the European Medicines Agency (HMPC)
precision: article-level; the Article 16a criteria and the Article 16b–16i structure were confirmed against the consolidated Directive 2001/83/EC text and the EUR-Lex record of Directive 2004/24/EC. The 30-year / 15-year traditional-use figures are stated from Article 16c(1)(c) and should be re-confirmed against the current consolidated text before being relied on for a filing.

title: Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 (DSHEA) — US framework for herbal dietary supplements
section: Pub. L. 103-417, amending the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (incl. FD&C Act ss. 201(ff), 413); cGMP at 21 CFR Part 111
summary: DSHEA is the US regime under which most herbal and botanical products are marketed as dietary supplements rather than drugs. A 'dietary ingredient' includes a vitamin, mineral, herb or other botanical, or amino acid. Under DSHEA the US FDA has no authority to approve a dietary supplement before it is marketed: manufacturers and distributors are themselves responsible for ensuring the product is safe and properly labelled, and may not market adulterated or misbranded products. The exception is a 'new dietary ingredient' (one not marketed in the US before 15 October 1994 and not present in the food supply in a form not chemically altered): the firm must notify FDA and submit safety information at least 75 days before marketing. Supplements must follow current good manufacturing practice under 21 CFR Part 111. A product represented as treating or curing a disease can be regulated as an unapproved drug rather than a supplement. For an Ayurvedic exporter this means a US launch of an herbal product is a labelling / cGMP / new-dietary-ingredient question, not a marketing-authorisation question — but Ayurvedic ingredients or extraction methods new to the US food supply can trigger the notification requirement, and 'traditional use' is not itself a US legal category.
version_date: enacted 25 October 1994; FDA guidance and rules continue to be updated
authority: US Congress; administered by the US Food and Drug Administration (Human Foods Program)
precision: framework-level; the no-pre-approval principle, ingredient categories and 75-day new-dietary-ingredient notification were confirmed against FDA's own dietary-supplement pages and guidance. Disease-claim and structure/function-claim rules and the exact cGMP requirements are summarised from the statute and 21 CFR Part 111 and should be checked against the current FDA text before a filing or label is finalised.

title: Regulation (EU) No 511/2014 — Nagoya Protocol compliance measures for users in the Union
section: Articles 4 (due diligence), 7 (checkpoints), 9 (checks); Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/1866
summary: The EU's implementation of the Nagoya Protocol's user-side compliance obligations. Anyone in the EU who utilises genetic resources or traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources must exercise due diligence to ascertain that access complied with the provider country's access-and-benefit-sharing rules and that mutually agreed terms were established where required; users must seek, keep and pass on the relevant information, and make a due-diligence declaration at defined stages of research funding or final product development. Relevant to an Indian Ayurvedic exporter: a product developed in the EU from Indian biological resources is checked against India's own ABS regime (the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and its rules), and an Indian internationally recognised certificate of compliance is the standard proof of legal access. The Regulation applies to resources accessed after the Protocol entered into force for the EU (12 October 2014), and it operates alongside, not instead of, EU herbal-medicine registration and any IP filing.
version_date: Regulation (EU) No 511/2014 of 16 April 2014; fully applicable from 12 October 2015; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/1866 of 13 October 2015
authority: European Parliament and Council of the EU; enforced by national competent authorities of EU Member States
precision: regulation-level; scope and the due-diligence obligation were confirmed against EUR-Lex's official summary and the Implementing Regulation's recitals. Article numbers and the exact declaration stages are given from the Regulation's structure and should be checked against the full EUR-Lex text before being relied on.

title: Trade secret / confidential information protection in India (common law, no dedicated statute)
section: Indian Contract Act, 1872, s.27 (agreements in restraint of trade, void save for the goodwill exception); equity and the tort/action of breach of confidence
summary: India has no dedicated trade-secret statute. Protection is granted entirely through common-law and contractual routes: (i) breach of confidence / equitable actions, recognised by Indian courts as an independent basis for relief distinct from patent or copyright law; (ii) contract — non-disclosure and confidentiality clauses in employment, consultancy, licensing and franchise agreements, enforceable subject to s.27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which voids agreements restraining a person from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business EXCEPT the limited goodwill-sale exception in the section's proviso (courts have separately upheld reasonable confidentiality obligations surviving employment, distinguishing them from a blanket non-compete); and (iii) equity, where a person who received confidential information without consent can still be restrained from using or disclosing it. A draft National Innovation Bill, 2008 (Ministry of Science and Technology) would have codified this position in a dedicated Chapter on 'Confidentiality and Confidential Information, Remedies and Offences' (its ss.8-9 largely restate the existing common-law position rather than creating new rights) — it was never introduced in Parliament and has lapsed; it should not be cited as current law. For an Ayurvedic manufacturer, this means a proprietary formulation, extraction process or supplier list is protectable only if actively kept secret and only through a signed confidentiality/NDA obligation or a breach-of-confidence claim — there is no registration, no certificate, and no government registry to point to, unlike patents or trademarks.
version_date: Indian Contract Act, 1872 (s.27, unamended on this point); National Innovation Bill, 2008 never enacted, lapsed
authority: Parliament of India (Contract Act); Indian courts (common-law breach-of-confidence doctrine); Ministry of Science and Technology (lapsed 2008 Bill, cited for context only)
precision: framework-level. The India Code link confirms the Contract Act s.27 text; the common-law discussion is supplemented by the fact-specific Delhi High Court decisions in IN-CASELAW-GUJARAT-BOTTLING, IN-CASELAW-BURLINGTON-1995, and IN-CASELAW-AMEX-PRIYA-PURI-2006. These cases do not create a dedicated trade-secret statute or guarantee protection for public information; confirm current law and facts before reliance.

title: WTO Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS)
section: Article 39 (Part II, Section 7 — Protection of Undisclosed Information)
summary: Sets the internationally agreed three-part test for what counts as protectable 'undisclosed information' (trade secrets), binding on India as a WTO member. Under Article 39.2, a person can prevent information from being disclosed, acquired or used without consent, in a manner contrary to honest commercial practices, so long as the information: (a) is secret, in that it is not generally known among or readily accessible to persons in the circles that normally deal with that kind of information; (b) has commercial value because it is secret; and (c) has been subject to reasonable steps, by the person lawfully in control of it, to keep it secret. Article 39.3 separately requires members to protect undisclosed test data submitted to obtain marketing approval for pharmaceutical or agricultural chemical products against unfair commercial use — directly relevant to clinical/safety data generated for a new Ayurvedic drug or phytopharmaceutical. TRIPS does not require a registration system for trade secrets (unlike patents or trademarks); it obliges members to make some legal remedy available, which is why India's common-law/contract route (see IN-TRADESECRET-COMMONLAW) is treated as TRIPS-compliant despite having no dedicated statute.
authority: World Trade Organization
precision: article-level, verified provision text (three-part test and the Art 39.3 test-data obligation confirmed against the WTO's own analytical index and treaty text)

title: Gujarat Bottling Co. Ltd. & Ors. v. Coca Cola Co. & Ors.
section: (1995) 5 SCC 545 [AIR 1995 SC 2372], Supreme Court of India
summary: The leading Supreme Court authority on the Section 27 (Indian Contract Act, 1872) restraint-of-trade doctrine as applied to negative covenants in a subsisting commercial agreement — the exact legal mechanism a confidentiality or non-compete clause protecting a trade secret relies on (see IN-TRADESECRET-COMMONLAW). Gujarat Bottling Co. (GBC) held a Coca Cola franchise to manufacture and bottle 'Gold Spot', 'Thums Up', 'Limca', 'Maaza' and allied brands under 1993/1994 agreements containing a negative covenant: GBC would not manufacture, bottle, sell or otherwise deal with any other brand's products during the subsistence of the agreement (including a one-year post-notice period). The Supreme Court upheld the covenant, holding that a restriction operating only during the currency of a contract — as opposed to after its termination — is not a 'restraint of trade' under s.27 at all: it is intra-contractual, designed to promote and facilitate the parties' trade rather than restrain it, so neither the statutory exception nor a reasonableness test needs to be reached. This is the precedent Sutradhara's own trade-secret guidance rests on: a confidentiality/exclusivity clause that operates only for the duration of an engagement (an NDA during a manufacturing collaboration, for instance) is on strong footing; the same clause purporting to bind a party after the relationship ends returns to s.27's general prohibition, save only the narrow goodwill-sale exception.
source_url: https://www.mondaq.com/article/1231912 (Mondaq — case commentary quoting the Supreme Court's holding)
authority: Supreme Court of India
precision: case-law analysis level — cited via secondary legal commentary (Mondaq, Lakshmikumaran & Sridharan's Corporate Amicus, and a dedicated case-note), consistent with this corpus's existing case-law entries, since no stable indiankanoon.org/court-registry link was confirmed live during this session. title: Tea Board, India v. ITC Limited
section: Calcutta High Court, decided 24 August 2011 (first reported GI-infringement decision in India)
summary: The first Indian court decision on infringement of a registered Geographical Indication, and a direct caution against over-reading what GI registration (see IN-GI-1999, which uses Darjeeling Tea as its own worked example) actually covers. The Tea Board of India, registered proprietor of the 'Darjeeling' GI and a certification mark for tea, sued ITC Limited over its 'Darjeeling Lounge' at a Kolkata hotel, alleging infringement and passing-off. The Calcutta High Court held the suit was time-barred under s.26(4) of the GI Act (a five-year limitation from when the proprietor becomes aware of the contested use), and went on to hold, on the merits, that the GI Act's protection — including its infringement provision, s.22 — is confined to 'goods': a GI registered for tea does not give its owner rights over the word 'Darjeeling' used for an unrelated service such as a hotel lounge. Directly relevant to an Ayurvedic GI holder (e.g. a registered regional herb or preparation): GI protection stops a competitor selling the same or similar GOODS under the protected name from outside the region, but does not by itself stop unrelated uses of the same word for services, other product categories, or generic/descriptive use — and a claim must be brought within five years of learning of the infringing use.
authority: Calcutta High Court
precision: case-law analysis level — cited via secondary legal commentary (Wolters Kluwer, Managing IP, BananaIP), consistent with this corpus's existing case-law entries; no stable indiankanoon.org/court-registry link was confirmed live during this session. The limitation holding, the goods-only scope of s.22, and the case's standing as the first Indian GI-infringement decision are independently corroborated across multiple contemporaneous legal-press sources.

title: Burlington Home Shopping Pvt. Ltd. v. Rajnish Chibber
section: Delhi High Court, R.C. Lahoti J., decided 20 October 1995; 61 (1995) DLT 6; 1995 (35) DRJ 335
summary: A mail-order company sought an interim injunction after a former employee allegedly used its compiled customer database to compete. The Delhi High Court found a strong prima facie copyright-infringement case on the record before it, including evidence that the defendant's database substantially copied the plaintiff's compilation, and restrained use of the plaintiff's exclusively owned customer list during the suit. The judgment discusses customer lists and business data as information that may be confidential, but its operative analysis rests on copying of a compiled database and copyright; it is not a rule that every customer list is automatically a trade secret. For an Ayurvedic business, the practical distinction is between a demonstrably protected, non-public compilation or formula and information independently ascertainable from public sources.
authority: Delhi High Court
precision: case-law text; fact-specific interlocutory injunction grounded in the record and copyright in a copied compilation. The confidentiality discussion should not be generalized into a standalone trade-secret rule.

title: American Express Bank Ltd. v. Ms. Priya Puri
section: Delhi High Court, Anil Kumar J., decided 24 May 2006
summary: American Express sought an injunction against a former wealth-management employee over alleged use of customer information and trade secrets. On the interlocutory record, the Delhi High Court found the bank's allegations of taking confidential files insufficiently supported and refused to use confidentiality claims to create a monopoly over customers or restrain ordinary competition and employment. The judgment distinguishes genuinely secret business information from general skill, experience, customer relationships, and information readily ascertainable by independent effort; it does not hold that properly protected confidential information can never be protected. It is a fact-specific caution to identify the information claimed as secret and prove access, secrecy measures, and misuse.
authority: Delhi High Court
precision: case-law text; interlocutory decision based on the evidence in that case. It distinguishes ascertainable customer relationships from protected confidential information and is not a categorical rule that customer data can never be secret.

title: European Medicines Agency — Herbal medicinal products and HMPC EU monographs
section: Traditional-use registration; well-established use; EU herbal monographs and EU list entries
summary: The European Medicines Agency describes the Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) role in establishing EU herbal monographs and an EU list for herbal substances and preparations. Monographs cover therapeutic uses and safe conditions for well-established and/or traditional use; applicants may use monographs and list entries in traditional-use registration applications, and demonstrating compliance with an EU list entry can remove the need to submit separate evidence of safe and traditional use. Monographs can also support well-established-use marketing authorisation. EMA distinguishes these therapeutic-use monographs from European Pharmacopoeia monographs, which address quality requirements; applicants must still establish product quality and use the applicable national authorization procedure. This is regulatory guidance for navigating the EU route, not a substitute for Directive 2001/83/EC or a product-specific assessment.
version_date: Page retrieved 30 September 2026; page date not specified
authority: European Medicines Agency; Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC)
precision: official regulatory overview; distinguishes the HMPC's therapeutic-use monographs from pharmacopoeial quality standards. The binding conditions remain those in the applicable EU legislation and national procedure.

title: US FDA — New Dietary Ingredient Notification Process
section: FD&C Act §413; 21 U.S.C. §350b (new dietary ingredient notification)
summary: The US FDA explains that manufacturers and distributors intending to market a dietary supplement containing a new dietary ingredient must notify FDA and provide the basis for concluding that the supplement will reasonably be expected to be safe under its labeled conditions of use. The statutory notice is generally due at least 75 days before marketing. Filing a notification is not FDA premarket approval or a finding that the product is safe. This is a separate compliance question from dietary-supplement cGMP, labeling, and whether disease claims cause a product to be regulated as a drug; the underlying statutory criteria and current FDA instructions should be checked for each ingredient and product.
authority: US Food and Drug Administration; US Congress (FD&C Act §413)
precision: official FDA process overview and statutory reference; the 75-day period is statutory. Not an FDA product approval or safety determination.

title: The Cosmetics Rules, 2020
section: General framework — manufacture, import, labelling, testing and sale of cosmetics; Rule 34 (labelling requirements)
summary: The Cosmetics Rules, 2020 (G.S.R. 763(E), notified 15 December 2020 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare) replace all cosmetics-specific provisions previously found in the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 and establish a standalone, comprehensive framework for the regulation of cosmetics in India under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. 'Cosmetic' is defined under Section 3(aaa) of the parent Act as any article intended to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled or sprayed on, or introduced into, or otherwise applied to, the human body for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering the appearance. Key provisions include: (i) Manufacture and import licensing requirements; (ii) Rule 34 — mandatory label declarations on both inner and outer labels (name of cosmetic; name and address of manufacturer; net contents in metric units; complete list of ingredients in decreasing order of predominance; batch number, date of manufacture and 'use before' expiry date; manufacturing licence number or registration certificate number; and specific precautionary statements such as 'For external use only' where applicable); (iii) requirement that many product categories conform to Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) specifications; (iv) an explicit bar on therapeutic or disease-cure claims on cosmetic labels — any such claim reclassifies the product as a drug, triggering the Drugs and Cosmetics Act / Ayurvedic drug-rules regime instead. Critically for Sutradhara users: a product containing Ayurvedic or herbal ingredients is regulated under these Cosmetics Rules — not the Ayurvedic drug or ASU provisions — if it is positioned as a cosmetic rather than a therapeutic/medicinal product. Products that straddle the cosmetic/drug boundary ('cosmeceuticals') have no separate legal category in Indian law and must be classified as either cosmetic or drug, with markedly different regulatory obligations and IP implications attaching to each choice.
version_date: G.S.R. 763(E), 15 December 2020; consolidated version updated November 2022
source_url: https://cdsco.gov.in/opencms/opencms/en/Acts-and-rules/Cosmetics-Rules/ (CDSCO — Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India — official Cosmetics Rules, 2020 page, with downloadable PDF of G.S.R. 763(E) dt. 15.12.2020 and consolidated November 2022 version; page confirmed live 1 October 2026)
authority: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India; CDSCO (Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation)
precision: rules-level citation, verified live on CDSCO's official Acts & Rules page; both the original gazette notification (G.S.R. 763(E), 2020-Dec-15, 2819 KB PDF) and the consolidated version (2022-Nov-21, 774 KB PDF) were confirmed as downloadable from the same official page at the time of retrieval; Rule 34 labelling requirements and the cosmetic/drug boundary are accurately characterised per the published rules text and CDSCO guidance

title: UK Human Medicines Regulations 2012 and MHRA Traditional Herbal Registration (THR)
section: Human Medicines Regulations 2012, Part 7; MHRA THR application guidance
summary: The United Kingdom operates a Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) route for certain herbal medicinal products, separately from the EU traditional-use registration route. MHRA says a product must be registered before it is marketed as a traditional herbal medicine; the simplified route is limited to minor conditions that do not require medical supervision, while products claiming to treat major conditions need a marketing authorisation. Applicants must provide evidence covering quality, safety and traditional use, including at least 30 years of medicinal use; the required geographic evidence differs by market scope, and MHRA says a wider range of countries may be considered for Great Britain-only applications. The Human Medicines Regulations 2012 provide the statutory framework. Whether a particular Ayurvedic product is a medicine, food supplement or cosmetic depends on its ingredients, presentation and claims; confirm the current MHRA guidance and legislation for the intended UK market before relying on this summary.
version_date: MHRA application guidance last updated 5 January 2024; Human Medicines Regulations 2012, Part 7
source_url: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/apply-for-a-traditional-herbal-registration-thr (Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, UK government guidance); https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2012/1916/part/7
authority: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency; UK Human Medicines Regulations 2012
precision: Official MHRA pathway guidance with the statutory framework identified. The exact eligibility of a product and accepted traditional-use evidence must be checked against current MHRA guidance and the applicable UK market route; this is not a product determination.

title: Canada Natural Health Products Regulations and licensed product database
section: Natural Health Products Regulations, SOR/2003-196; product licensing and Licensed Natural Health Products Database (LNHPD)
summary: Canada regulates natural health products (NHPs), including products identified by Health Canada as Ayurvedic (East Indian) medicines. A product must generally hold a product licence before sale; licensed products receive an eight-digit Natural Product Number (NPN) or, for certain homeopathic medicines, a DIN-HM number. Health Canada describes pre-market review of safety, efficacy and quality, and site licensing and good manufacturing practice requirements for relevant parties. Its Licensed Natural Health Products Database (LNHPD) provides information on licensed products, including licence holder, ingredients, recommended use and risks, and is updated regularly. A database listing or licence is not a determination that a product is lawful in another country or that it can make any desired claim; check the current Canadian regulations, product record and applicable import/export rules.
version_date: Natural Health Products Regulations, SOR/2003-196; official Health Canada guidance checked 2 October 2026
source_url: https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/sor-2003-196/ (Justice Laws Website, current consolidated regulations); https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/drugs-health-products/natural-non-prescription/regulation/about-products.html (Health Canada, About Natural Health Products); https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/drugs-health-products/natural-non-prescription/applications-submissions/product-licensing/licensed-natural-health-products-database.html (Health Canada, LNHPD overview and database)
